title: Four Routes From OmniScan Data to a Signed Inspection Report
description: OmniScan writes .opd, .odat and .nde; EPOCH writes CSV and XML. What each format carries, and the exact route from acquisition file to a client deliverable.
h1: Getting OmniScan and EPOCH Data Into a Client-Ready Inspection Report
answer: OmniScan data reaches a finished report by one of four routes: OmniPC's built-in indication table exported as HTML, a C-scan CSV export dropped into a reporting template, a direct HDF5 read of the .nde open file format, or the OpenView SDK for legacy .opd and .odat files. Which route is open to you is decided entirely by the format your instrument writes.
expansion: An OmniScan does not produce a report. It produces an acquisition file, and every workflow question downstream is really a question about which file you have. OmniScan X3 and X3 64 running MXU 5.11 and later write .nde, the Open File Format NDE, which Evident built on HDF5 with a JSON descriptor, so any tool that reads HDF5 reaches the data without Evident software. Earlier MX2, SX and MXU 4.x units write .opd, and X3 acquisition through WeldSight uses .odat. Those two remain proprietary and are reached through OmniPC, WeldSight or the OpenView SDK. Conventional units such as the EPOCH 650 sidestep the problem by exporting datalogger contents as .csv or .xml. The report itself is assembled from three ingredients: the indication table, the calibration and technique record, and the images. Getting those three into a template is the whole job.
source: Evident (formerly Olympus IMS) Open File Format NDE FAQ and OpenView SDK release notes 1.1.98.0; ASTM E2339-21, Standard Practice for Digital Imaging and Communication in Nondestructive Evaluation (DICONDE)

table.note: Evident does not support conversion between these acquisition formats. Choose the analysis and reporting path that matches the format your fleet already writes, rather than planning a migration between them.

facets.q: Can OmniPC export a phased array report directly to PDF?
facets.a: OmniPC and the OmniScan onboard reporting function generate an HTML report containing the indication table, comments, weld profile with RayTracing and high-resolution images. PDF is produced by printing or converting that HTML. Companies that need a specific client cover page, revision block or signature panel usually rebuild the report outside OmniPC and use the HTML output as the source of the numbers.

facets.q: What is the difference between .opd, .odat and .nde files?
facets.a: They are three generations of OmniScan acquisition file. The .opd format belongs to MX2, SX and MXU 4.x era instruments and opens in OmniPC. The .odat format is OmniScan X3 acquisition data used by WeldSight. The .nde format is the Open File Format NDE, written by OmniScan X3 and X3 64 on MXU 5.11 and later, built on HDF5 with JSON. Evident does not support converting between them.

facets.q: Can you open a .nde file in Python?
facets.a: Yes. Evident states that any software able to open and read HDF5 or JSON files can read .nde data, which means h5py or PyTables in Python, or the HDF5 tooling in MATLAB. That is the deliberate design intent of the Open File Format NDE: it removes the requirement for proprietary Evident software before you can reach the underlying dataset for scripting and automated reporting.

facets.q: Does the OmniScan C-scan CSV export include A-scan waveforms?
facets.a: No. The documented export applies to the C-scan window and writes every data point in that view, giving position with amplitude or thickness per cell. Full A-scan waveform arrays are not part of that export. If a client deliverable requires representative A-scans, capture them as images from the analysis software, or read the waveform arrays from the .nde HDF5 container or through the OpenView SDK.

facets.q: How do you get EPOCH 650 readings into Excel?
facets.a: The EPOCH 650 exports saved datalogger contents as .csv or .xml directly from the instrument, and GageView Pro transfers thickness and amplitude data from the instrument to Excel, Word or similar programs over the USB client port. Either route gives you a tabular file with the file and ID structure intact, which is enough to drive a thickness survey report template without manual transcription.

facets.q: Do you need WeldSight, or is OmniPC enough for a weld report?
facets.a: Both provide standard post-process corrections — gain, Auto 80%, index and scan offsets, gate editing — and both provide a basic indication table and reporting. WeldSight adds volumetric data merging, a geometry-based weld gate, advanced TOFD tools including SAFT and lateral wave processing, an analysis dashboard with missing-data statistics, and 3D and polar visualisation. Routine coded weld work is served by OmniPC; complex geometry and merged-scan sizing justify WeldSight.

sections.heading: Decide the deliverable before you open the file
paragraphs: The mistake that costs the most hours is starting from the acquisition file and asking what can be done with it. Start from the other end. Write down exactly what the client receives: a cover sheet with contract and procedure references, a technique or calibration record, an indication table with location and sizing, representative imagery, an acceptance statement against the governing code, and a Level II or Level III signature. That list is the specification for everything upstream.

Once the deliverable is fixed, each element traces back to a source. The indication table comes from the analysis software or from a parsed dataset. Calibration and technique parameters live inside the acquisition file and inside your procedure library. Images come from the analysis view. The acceptance statement comes from a human reading the code. Only two of those four are automatable, and knowing which two prevents you from buying a tool to solve a problem it cannot solve.

This ordering also decides how much file-format work is worth doing. If the client accepts an OmniPC HTML report with a cover sheet stapled on, the whole problem collapses to a formatting exercise. If the client wants tabulated thickness grids, trend comparison against a previous outage, or data loaded into an integrity database, you need the numbers themselves, and the format question becomes the project.

sections.heading: What each OmniScan file format actually carries
paragraphs: An OmniScan acquisition file is not a report and was never intended to be one. It is a dense record of the inspection: the beam configuration, the gates, the encoder positions, the calibration state, and the amplitude and time data for every focal law at every scan position. That richness is why the files are large, and why the same file can be reanalysed years later with different gates and different sizing criteria without going back to the weld.

Three formats matter in practice. The .opd file belongs to the MX2, SX and MXU 4.x generation and is the format most existing archives are stored in. The .odat file is OmniScan X3 acquisition data, the format WeldSight is built around. The .nde file is the Open File Format NDE, written by OmniScan X3 and X3 64 units running MXU 5.11 onboard software and later.

Evident is explicit that conversion between these formats is not supported. That single fact shapes fleet strategy more than any software choice. A company running mixed-generation OmniScans will be running two or three analysis paths in parallel, and any reporting pipeline has to accept that rather than assume a single normalised input. Plan the pipeline around whichever format your newest instruments write, and keep the legacy path alive for archive retrieval.

sections.heading: The .nde open file format removed the biggest blocker
paragraphs: For most of the phased array era, getting numbers out of an OmniScan file meant using Evident software or licensing a development kit. The Open File Format NDE changed that. Evident built .nde on HDF5, the open hierarchical data format, with a JSON descriptor layer, and states plainly that any software capable of opening and reading HDF5 or JSON files can also open .nde data. Files can be accessed without proprietary Evident software.

The practical consequence is large. A Python script using h5py, or a MATLAB session, can walk the file structure, pull the amplitude arrays and the acquisition parameters, and hand both to a reporting engine. That makes automated indication tables, batch thickness grid generation and integrity-database ingestion into ordinary engineering work rather than a vendor negotiation. It also means archived data stays readable independent of any single vendor's software roadmap.

Two cautions apply. First, readable is not the same as self-explanatory: you still have to learn the group and dataset layout before the numbers mean anything, and that is a real piece of work. Second, version compatibility is tracked per MXU release. Evident's OpenView SDK release notes, for example, record version 1.1.98.0 adding compatibility with OmniScan X3 MXU 5.17 .nde data files. Pin your instrument firmware and your parsing library together, and revalidate after either changes.

sections.heading: Legacy .opd and .odat still need vendor software or the SDK
paragraphs: Most companies with a decade of phased array history are sitting on .opd archives, and those files are not open. The supported routes are OmniPC for analysis and reporting, and the OpenView SDK for programmatic access. Public ndt.net forum threads asking how to convert .opd to raw data are long-running precisely because there is no sanctioned conversion path, and any workaround you find in a forum is unvalidated for code work.

The OpenView SDK is the honest answer for anyone who genuinely needs bulk access to legacy files. It is a development kit, which means a C++ or C# developer, a compatibility matrix to respect, and a test suite proving that what you extracted matches what OmniPC displays. That last step is not optional. If your extracted amplitude does not reproduce the analysis software's reading on a known reference, you cannot put the output in front of a client.

For .odat, WeldSight is the intended path. Newer MXU and OmniPC versions can open earlier acquisition files, but Evident notes that newer analysis features may not function with them. Treat that as a hard constraint on reanalysis campaigns: a file acquired under an older software generation may not support the sizing tools your current procedure calls for, and you need to know that before you promise a client a re-evaluation.

sections.heading: The C-scan CSV export, and what it leaves behind
paragraphs: The fastest route from OmniScan data to a numeric deliverable is the C-scan CSV export, and it is under-used. In OmniPC you right-click the C-scan window; on an OmniScan running MXU 4.2 or later you press and hold it. Select Export, and a CSV is written to the computer or to the SD card. Evident describes the output as containing every single data point from the inspection alongside the inspection information.

That file is immediately useful. Dropped into Excel, conditional formatting turns a thickness C-scan into a readable corrosion map in about a minute. Position, average thickness, minimum thickness and the area below a threshold all fall out of ordinary spreadsheet functions. The same file feeds pipeline burst-pressure calculators and fitness-for-service tooling without any transcription step, which removes the single largest source of reporting error.

Be clear about what does not come with it. The export is scoped to the C-scan view, so full A-scan waveform arrays are not in the file. Gate settings, wedge and probe details and the calibration record still have to be carried across from the setup or the analysis software. The CSV is a numbers pipe, not a complete inspection record, and a report built only from it will fail a document review.

sections.heading: EPOCH 650 and conventional UT take a different path
paragraphs: Conventional flaw detection and thickness work never had the format problem, because the data volume is small enough to stay tabular. The EPOCH 650 carries an onboard datalogger for calibration and inspection files with up to 100,000 points of memory, and saved data exports as .csv or .xml directly. GageView Pro provides the PC-side route, moving thickness or amplitude data to Excel, Word or similar programs over the USB client port.

This makes thickness survey reporting the easiest automation win in most NDT shops. A CML list goes out to the instrument as a file and ID structure, readings come back in the same structure, and a template joins them to previous readings to produce remaining-life and corrosion-rate columns. Nothing about that requires an SDK, and a competent Excel or Python build does it end to end.

The EPOCH 650 also records up to eight minutes of live A-scan at 60 frames per second, reviewable on the instrument or exported for PC review. That is evidence, not report data, but it changes what you can defend later. When a client disputes an indication call, a recorded A-scan sequence with the calibration file attached settles the argument in a way that a static screenshot does not.

sections.heading: Where DICONDE fits, and where it does not
paragraphs: DICONDE is the standard people reach for when they want vendor-neutral inspection data, and it is frequently misapplied. It is defined in ASTM E2339, Standard Practice for Digital Imaging and Communication in Nondestructive Evaluation, and it is a harmonisation of NDE imaging with the NEMA DICOM standard used in medical imaging. Its purpose is to preserve the technique parameters alongside the image data so that both survive changes in NDE technology.

Its strength is archival and cross-modality viewing. The standard is written so that CT, CR, ultrasonic, infrared and eddy current data can be displayed on a single conformant workstation regardless of the acquiring modality. For a company running digital radiography alongside other methods, that is a genuine long-term asset-integrity advantage, and it is why DICONDE dominates in DR and CT environments.

What DICONDE is not is a reporting format. It carries the image and the acquisition parameters; it does not carry your indication table, your acceptance criteria or your signature block. Nor is it the native output of an OmniScan. Treat DICONDE as the archive layer beneath your reporting layer, not as a substitute for it, and do not let a client specification that names DICONDE be read as a requirement your phased array fleet has failed to meet.

sections.heading: The four practical routes from instrument to client PDF
paragraphs: Route one is the vendor report. Generate the indication table in OmniPC or on the instrument, add comments and images, output HTML, print to PDF, attach a cover sheet. It is fast, it is defensible because the numbers are the analysis software's own, and it is inflexible. Companies whose clients accept it should stop here, because every alternative costs engineering time to gain formatting control they may not need.

Route two is CSV plus a template. Export the C-scan CSV or the EPOCH datalogger file, load it into a controlled Excel or reporting-engine template that already contains your cover page, procedure references and acceptance logic, and paste in analysis screenshots. This is where most mid-sized shops land. It removes transcription error, it keeps report branding under your control, and it needs no developer.

Route three is a programmatic pipeline against .nde. Parse the HDF5 file, extract indications and parameters, and render the report from a template engine with the images attached. Route four is the same idea against .opd or .odat through the OpenView SDK, which costs materially more effort. Route three is worth building when report volume is high and formats are standardised; route four is worth building only when a legacy archive has to be reprocessed at scale.

sections.heading: What no tool does for you automatically
paragraphs: No software decides whether an indication is rejectable. Acceptance is a judgement made by a qualified individual against a governing code and a written procedure, and every credible workflow keeps a human in that position. A reporting tool can pre-populate the amplitude, the depth, the length and the position, and it can flag values against thresholds you configured, but the accept or reject call and the signature that follows are personnel actions, not software actions.

No software reconstructs missing setup information either. If the acquisition file was saved without the correct probe, wedge, weld geometry or calibration block details entered, no downstream parser invents them. The cheapest quality intervention in the whole chain is enforcing complete setup metadata at the instrument, before the scan, because everything downstream is a copy of what was entered there.

And no import path fixes a bad scan. Missing data from lost encoder coupling, insufficient coverage of the required volume, or a calibration that drifted mid-shift will still be missing after the smartest parsing in the world. WeldSight's analysis dashboard reporting missing-data statistics exists because this is a real and frequent failure. Automation multiplies the quality of the data you acquired; it does not raise it.

sections.heading: Build the pipeline in-house or buy it
paragraphs: Building in-house is genuinely viable now that .nde is HDF5-based. A single competent Python developer, a documented file layout, and a validation set of files with known OmniPC readings will get a working indication-table extractor in weeks rather than months. The ongoing cost is what surprises people: firmware updates, new instrument generations, new client report formats and staff turnover all land on whoever wrote the script.

Buying shifts that maintenance burden but introduces a fit question. Ask any vendor exactly which formats they ingest, at which MXU versions, and what happens to your .opd archive. Ask whether their report templates are editable by your Level III or only by their support team. Ask whether reports can be produced and signed offline at a plant with no connectivity, because a great deal of NDT work happens inside facilities where phones are prohibited.

Atlantis builds the reporting layer for NDT service companies around this exact chain — ingest from exported CSV and HDF5-based .nde data plus captured imagery, method templates aligned to ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practices and ISO documentation requirements, offline mobile capture, and configurable client report formats — and integrates it with an Odoo-based ERP so certification, calibration and invoicing sit behind the same record. It is affordable, accessible and fully customisable, and it is scoped per company. Request a demo or a quote at /contact or info@atlantisndt.com, and bring three real files with you so the fit question gets answered with your data.

sections.heading: A short checklist before you commit to a workflow
paragraphs: Inventory your instruments by MXU version, not by model name, because the format boundary sits at MXU 5.11 for .nde and MXU 4.2 for the C-scan CSV export. Count how many of your units fall each side of those lines. That number tells you whether you are building one pipeline or two, and it is the single most useful piece of information in the whole exercise.

Take three representative jobs — a weld PAUT job, a corrosion mapping job, a conventional thickness survey — and walk each one end to end by hand, timing every step. Most companies discover that the expensive step is not data extraction at all but assembling the cover sheet, chasing procedure revision numbers, and getting the Level III signature. Automating the wrong step delivers nothing.

Finally, validate before you deploy. Whatever route you choose, prove on a reference file that the numbers in your generated report match the numbers the analysis software displays, and keep that comparison as a controlled record. It costs a day, it satisfies auditors, and it is the difference between an efficiency gain and a systematic reporting error replicated across every job you issue.

faq.q: Which OmniScan software version writes the .nde open file format?
faq.a: Evident documents the Open File Format NDE as written by OmniScan X3 and OmniScan X3 64 flaw detectors running MXU 5.11 onboard software and later. Files are readable in MXU and OmniPC, and by any software able to open HDF5 or JSON. Instruments on earlier firmware write .opd or .odat instead, and Evident does not support conversion between the formats.

faq.q: Is DICONDE required for phased array ultrasonic data?
faq.a: DICONDE, defined in ASTM E2339, is an imaging and communication practice that preserves technique parameters alongside image data and permits CT, CR, ultrasonic, infrared and eddy current data to be viewed on one conformant workstation. It is an archival and interoperability standard, not a reporting format, and it is not the native output of an OmniScan. Requirements come from the client specification or contract, not from the method.

faq.q: Can inspection reports be produced offline in the field?
faq.a: Yes, and for many facilities it is mandatory. OmniPC and the OmniScan onboard reporting function run without connectivity, and CSV or XML exports write to an SD card or laptop. Any platform layered on top has to capture, store and sign locally, then sync when connectivity returns. Verify this behaviour on a real device before deployment rather than accepting a feature-list claim.

faq.q: Who signs a report generated from OmniScan data?
faq.a: The qualified individual whose certification level the governing procedure requires — commonly a Level II for interpretation and a Level III for procedure approval and technique qualification, as set out in your employer's written practice under ASNT SNT-TC-1A or your ISO 9712 scheme. Software populates the data and can enforce a review-and-release sequence, but the accept or reject decision and the signature remain personnel actions.

faq.q: Does Atlantis reporting software import OmniScan files?
faq.a: Atlantis builds ingest against exported CSV data, HDF5-based .nde files and captured imagery, with the exact scope configured per customer's instrument fleet and MXU versions. There is no universal one-click import for proprietary .opd or .odat, and any vendor claiming otherwise should be asked to demonstrate it on your files. Bring three representative datasets to a scoping call. Request a demo or quote at /contact or info@atlantisndt.com.

faq.q: What is the fastest improvement if we change only one thing?
faq.a: Enforce complete setup metadata at the instrument before scanning — probe, wedge, weld geometry, calibration block and operator — and switch thickness reporting to the datalogger CSV or XML export instead of transcription. Together those two changes remove the largest source of reporting error and the largest block of administrative time, and neither requires new software or a developer.

title: Six Floodlight Software Alternatives, Compared on What Actually Differs
description: Floodlight leads North American NDT inspection management. Compare it against AgileNDT, DRIVE NDT, InspectionsTrack and ERP-based options on the axes that decide.
h1: Floodlight Software Alternatives for NDT Inspection Companies
answer: Floodlight Software, founded in 2019 and based in Cary, North Carolina, covers dispatch, offline mobile capture, a drag-and-drop form builder, certification tracking and quote-to-cash with QuickBooks and Xero connectors. The alternatives worth evaluating differ on four axes: offline reliability in the field, depth of personnel certification and calibration tracking, accounting and ERP reach, and how far the platform bends to your existing workflow.
expansion: Floodlight Software is the reference point in North American NDT inspection management because it covers the full operational span rather than reporting alone — dispatch, a drag-and-drop form builder, offline mobile capture, client and work-order management, a customer portal, equipment management, job quoting and a REST API with QuickBooks and Xero connectors. Its published claim is 24 administrative hours saved per inspector per month. Alternatives win on narrower ground. AgileNDT, run from Scotland since 2011, leads with controlled report review-and-release and auditable technician qualifications. DRIVE NDT, built in Germany, organises around ISO 9712 traceability across eleven or more methods. InspectionsTrack extends beyond NDT into lifting gear, drill pipe and PRV work for oil and gas operators. ERP-based approaches, including the Atlantis build on Odoo 18, trade out-of-the-box polish for the ability to model your own workflow. Choose on the constraint that is currently costing you money.

facets.q: Is Floodlight Software only suitable for large inspection companies?
facets.a: No. Its module structure — dispatch, mobile, form builder, client management, quoting, equipment — scales down to a single crew, and the customer portal is often what wins small firms their first enterprise client. The real constraint is not headcount but process maturity: a company with no standard forms, no dispatch discipline and no certification register gains less from any platform than from fixing those first.

facets.q: Which Floodlight alternatives genuinely work offline?
facets.a: Floodlight publicly documents offline data capture with local storage and automatic sync on iOS and Android, and the Atlantis mobile capture layer is built offline-first. Instrument vendor software such as OmniPC runs entirely on a local laptop. Cloud-first platforms including AgileNDT and DRIVE NDT should be tested directly, because degraded-connectivity behaviour is rarely described precisely in marketing material and matters enormously inside refineries and plants.

facets.q: Can an ERP replace dedicated NDT inspection software?
facets.a: Only if the reporting layer is built properly on top of it. An ERP handles projects, invoicing, inventory, purchasing and document control natively, and certification and calibration map cleanly onto ERP record types with expiry logic. What an ERP does not supply out of the box is method-specific field forms, offline capture and code-referenced report templates. The Odoo-based Atlantis approach adds exactly that layer rather than replacing the ERP.

facets.q: What integrations should an NDT platform have?
facets.a: Accounting first — QuickBooks and Xero are the connectors Floodlight publishes, and matching your existing ledger avoids a second migration. Then a documented REST API, because every inspection company eventually needs data pushed into a client's asset-integrity system. Then file ingest from your instrument fleet. Single sign-on and a customer portal matter once you serve enterprise clients with their own IT requirements.

facets.q: How long does migrating off a legacy reporting system take?
facets.a: Budget the migration around form rebuilding, not data transfer. Rebuilding twenty to forty method-specific forms with correct code references and acceptance logic is the work, and it needs a Level III's time, not just an administrator's. Historical reports are usually archived as PDFs rather than re-imported. Run the new platform in parallel on live jobs for one full billing cycle before switching off the old one.

facets.q: Which platform handles ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice requirements?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice; your employer's written practice is the governing document, so the question is whether a platform can hold what your written practice states. Floodlight publicly documents tracking of inspector levels I–III, expiration dates and recertification hours with automatic alerts. AgileNDT provides an auditable certifications module, DRIVE NDT organises around ISO 9712, and ERP-based approaches model the rules directly. All are workable; the difference is configurability.

sections.heading: What Floodlight does well, stated plainly
paragraphs: Any honest comparison starts by conceding the leader's strengths. Floodlight Software is built specifically for non-destructive testing and industrial inspection rather than adapted from generic field service, and its module set reflects that: dispatch for scheduling and technician management, a mobile app for iOS and Android with offline data capture and automatic sync, a drag-and-drop digital form builder, client and work-order management, a customer portal, equipment management, job quoting and cost management.

The method coverage is the expected UT, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET, with forms and compliance templates referencing ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ASME, AWS, API and ASTM documents. Certification tracking covers inspector levels I through III with expiration dates, recertification hours and automatic alerts. Integrations run through a REST API with QuickBooks and Xero connectors. The company was founded in 2019 and is based in Cary, North Carolina.

Its headline claim is 24 administrative hours saved per inspector per month. Treat that as a vendor figure rather than an independent benchmark — it is a marketing number, and the components published alongside it do not sum cleanly to the headline. The underlying point stands regardless: the time sink in NDT companies is administration, not inspection, and a platform that removes re-keying earns its place. Verify the magnitude against your own timesheets.

sections.heading: The four axes that actually separate these platforms
paragraphs: Feature grids on Capterra and GetApp make every platform look identical because every vendor ticks every box. The differences are in depth, not presence. Four axes decide real outcomes, and a shortlist built on them will be more useful than one built on a hundred-row checklist.

Offline capture is first, because it either works inside a refinery or the platform is unusable there. Certification and calibration depth is second, because that is what fails an audit. Back-office reach is third — whether the platform stops at the report or follows through to the invoice and the ledger you already run. Configurability is fourth: whether your Level III can edit a report template and a form without a support ticket.

A fifth consideration sits underneath all of them: company size and process maturity. A four-person shop and a two-hundred-technician contractor have almost nothing in common in what they need from software, and the same platform will be right for one and wrong for the other. Any comparison that produces a single winner regardless of who is asking is not a comparison, it is an advertisement.

sections.heading: Offline capture is the axis that breaks deployments
paragraphs: More NDT software rollouts fail on connectivity than on features. Technicians work inside vessels, in tank farms, on offshore installations and in plants with intrinsic safety restrictions and no signal. If capture requires a live connection, work gets recorded on paper and typed in later, which reintroduces exactly the transcription cost the platform was bought to remove — plus a new licence fee.

Floodlight publicly documents offline functionality with local data storage and automatic syncing on its mobile app, which is the correct architecture. Atlantis builds its capture layer offline-first for the same reason. Instrument vendor software runs on a local laptop and is offline by definition. Cloud-first platforms including AgileNDT and DRIVE NDT are described primarily in cloud terms, so their degraded-connectivity behaviour should be established directly with the vendor rather than assumed.

Test it properly. Put the app on a real device, enable airplane mode, complete a full inspection including photographs and signatures, close the app, reopen it, then reconnect and confirm nothing was lost and nothing duplicated. Then repeat with two technicians editing related records offline simultaneously and check how the conflict resolves. Twenty minutes of that testing is worth more than any demo.

sections.heading: Certification and calibration tracking: the audit-day test
paragraphs: The scenario that decides this axis is a client auditor asking, without notice, for evidence that the technician who signed a report from eight months ago held current certification in that method on that date, and that the instrument used was within calibration. If producing that takes more than a minute, the tracking is decorative.

Floodlight documents monitoring of inspector qualifications, levels I through III, expiration dates and recertification hours with automatic alerts, plus equipment and parts inventory tracking. AgileNDT's certifications module is positioned around keeping technician qualifications visible and auditable, alongside a controlled report review-and-release process — which is the other half of the same audit question. DRIVE NDT organises personnel and equipment records around ISO 9712 traceability, which suits European scheme-certified operations.

The subtlety is that ASNT SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a rule. Your employer's written practice governs, and written practices differ on vision test intervals, practical examination requirements and how interrupted service is handled. So the real question is not whether a platform tracks certifications but whether it can hold your written practice's specific rules. Ask each vendor to configure one of your genuinely awkward cases during the trial.

sections.heading: Back-office reach, and where quote-to-cash lands
paragraphs: An inspection company's profitability problem is rarely in the field. It is in the gap between work performed and cash collected: quotes issued late, jobs closed without all consumables and travel captured, invoices raised weeks after the report went out, and no reliable view of margin by client or by job type. A platform that stops at the report leaves that gap intact.

Floodlight closes it inside the platform with job quoting, work-order management, cost management for delivery metrics and profitability, and a REST API with QuickBooks and Xero connectors. AgileNDT includes quotes, billing and inventory modules. DRIVE NDT includes cost calculation and billing built onto its order management core. InspectionsTrack focuses more on inspection registers, certificates and report generation across a broader oil and gas asset scope.

The ERP-based route inverts the design. Rather than a field platform reaching into accounting, the accounting, project, inventory, purchasing and document control functions are the foundation, and inspection capture and reporting are built on top of them. That is more work at the start and materially stronger once you are running multi-site projects, subcontractors, consumables inventory and ISO 9001 document control from the same record set.

sections.heading: The ERP-first alternative, and when it wins
paragraphs: An Odoo-based approach is a genuinely different answer, not a cheaper version of the same answer. Odoo 18 supplies projects, timesheets, invoicing, purchasing, inventory, HR and document control as native modules. Technician certifications become records with expiry logic and automated reminders. Equipment calibration becomes a maintenance schedule. Inspection reports become documents attached to project and asset records that the finance and quality functions already work inside.

It wins in three situations. When your workflow does not resemble anyone else's — unusual approval chains, client-specific report formats, multi-currency multi-entity operations — a configurable ERP bends where a fixed platform will not. When you already run a heavy back office and cannot tolerate a second system of record. And when you need one dataset feeding quality, operations and finance rather than three exports reconciled monthly.

It loses when you want to be productive next week. Out of the box, Odoo knows nothing about phased array, weld maps or SNT-TC-1A, and someone has to build that. That build is exactly what Atlantis packages as a pre-configured Odoo 18 for NDT companies, but it remains a configuration project with a scoping phase, not a download. If your requirement is standard and your timeline is short, a purpose-built platform is the more honest recommendation.

sections.heading: Company size changes the right answer
paragraphs: Below roughly five technicians, the correct answer is often none of these. Well-controlled Word or Excel templates, a disciplined folder structure and a calendar of certification and calibration expiries cost nothing and work. The failure mode at this size is not inefficiency but inconsistency, and that is solved by template control rather than by software. Revisit when report volume or client audit pressure makes manual tracking unreliable.

Between roughly five and fifty technicians, dedicated platforms pay for themselves quickly, and this is Floodlight's core territory alongside AgileNDT and DRIVE NDT. The binding constraint at this size is administrative time and audit readiness. Prioritise offline capture, form configurability and accounting integration, and resist buying capability you will not use for three years.

Above fifty technicians, or across multiple sites and legal entities, the integration question dominates. You will have an existing ERP or accounting system, client asset-integrity systems to feed, and enough report volume that programmatic ingest of instrument data becomes worthwhile. At that scale, evaluate on API quality and data ownership as heavily as on features, and take seriously how you would extract everything if you left.

sections.heading: Where Atlantis fits, honestly
paragraphs: Atlantis is not the default answer on this page and should not be treated as one. If your requirement is a standard North American NDT service company workflow, you want it running quickly, and QuickBooks or Xero is your ledger, Floodlight is a strong and well-matched product and there is no reason to pretend otherwise. Buying the incumbent when the incumbent fits is a good decision.

Atlantis is the better fit in three specific cases. When reporting and ERP must share one record set rather than sync between two systems. When your report formats, approval chains or client requirements are unusual enough that a fixed template library becomes a constant fight. And when the scope extends past inspection management into digital twin visualisation of assets with inspection history attached, which is a different category of requirement altogether.

The commercial position is affordable, accessible and fully customisable, scoped per company rather than sold from a price list. That is a deliberate consequence of the configuration model: what you need built determines the engagement. Bring your three most awkward report formats and your written practice to a scoping call and the fit question gets answered concretely. Request a demo or a quote at /contact or info@atlantisndt.com.

sections.heading: How to run a two-week evaluation that actually decides
paragraphs: Shortlist three, not seven. Pick one purpose-built North American platform, one alternative that leads on the axis you care most about, and one configurable option. More than three and every trial becomes shallow, which is how companies end up choosing on demo polish rather than fit.

Give each vendor identical material: your three most complex report formats, your written practice, a real job with photographs and instrument exports, and one deliberately awkward certification case. Then run a real job on each platform, in the field, on the technician's own device, with connectivity disabled. Have the technician do it, not the office. Time the full cycle from dispatch to invoice-ready.

Score on five things and nothing else: did offline capture survive a full job intact; can your Level III edit a report template unaided; does the certification register answer the audit-day question in under a minute; does the invoice reach your existing ledger without re-keying; and can you export everything you put in, in a usable format, if you leave. A platform that passes all five is a good decision at any size. One that fails the last is a risk regardless of how well it demonstrates.

faq.q: Who are Floodlight Software's main competitors?
faq.a: Category listings name Intellect, InspectionXpert and AgileNDT among alternatives. In practice, NDT service companies also evaluate DRIVE NDT for ISO 9712-oriented European operations, InspectionsTrack for oil and gas scopes extending into lifting gear and drill pipe, ERP-based builds such as the Atlantis configuration on Odoo 18, and instrument vendor analysis software where deep method-level analysis rather than business management is the requirement.

faq.q: Does Floodlight Software work without a signal in the field?
faq.a: Floodlight publicly documents offline functionality with local data storage and automatic syncing in its iOS and Android mobile app, covering UT thickness readings, RT shot logs, MT and PT checklists and visual inspection reports. Verify the specific behaviour on your own devices during a trial, including photograph capture, signatures and conflict resolution when two technicians edit related records while disconnected.

faq.q: Is there a good alternative for a small North American NDT firm?
faq.a: Below roughly five technicians, disciplined Word and Excel templates with a controlled folder structure and a certification expiry calendar remain a defensible answer and cost nothing. Above that, Floodlight scales down well, and a configured Odoo-based build suits firms with unusual workflows or an existing back office. The trigger to move is audit pressure or report volume, not headcount alone.

faq.q: Can I keep QuickBooks if I switch platforms?
faq.a: Floodlight publishes a REST API with QuickBooks and Xero connectors, so the ledger stays in place. Other platforms include their own billing modules, which means deciding whether invoicing lives in the platform or in your accounting system and syncing accordingly. ERP-based approaches usually replace the accounting system entirely, which is a larger decision and should be evaluated as one.

faq.q: What is the single most common evaluation mistake?
faq.a: Choosing on a scripted demo instead of a real job. Demos run on good connectivity, clean data and the vendor's own forms. The failures that matter appear when a technician loses signal inside a vessel, when a Level III tries to edit a report template unaided, and when an auditor asks for certification evidence from eight months ago. Test those three specifically.

title: Outside NDT Level III: Approves Everything Except the Signature
description: Under SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 an outside Level III writes your practice, sets and grades exams and approves procedures. Your company still signs the certificate.
h1: What an Outside NDT Level III Can and Cannot Do for Your Certification Program
answer: No. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189, certification is an act of the employer. An outside Level III writes and approves your written practice, prepares, administers and grades examinations, approves procedures, and audits the program. An officer of your company signs the certification record. NAS 410 differs only in that it names a Responsible Level 3 in writing, who may be contracted.
expansion: The distinction that decides every audit finding here is qualify versus certify. Qualification is evidentiary: training hours delivered, documented experience, a general examination, a method examination, a practical demonstration, a current vision test. Certification is administrative: a signed record in which an employer declares that a named person meets that employer's written practice for a stated method and level. SNT-TC-1A places the written practice with the employer at paragraph 5.1 and requires the employer's NDT Level III to review and approve it at 5.5. An outside Level III can occupy the Level III role in that sentence end to end, writing the practice, setting and grading the examinations, approving procedures and auditing the program, while the certifying signature stays inside your company. Paragraph 7.4 makes the parallel point about outsourced training: use whoever you like, but the employer remains responsible for assuring the training met the written practice.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition), paras 1.4, 5.1, 5.5, 5.6, 7.4, 8.1.1, Sections 8, 12 and 13; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 (2024); AIA NAS 410 Rev. 6, para 4.5; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120(e).

table.note: CAN and CANNOT describe authority, not competence. A contracted Level III may perform every technical act in rows 1-5 and still never appear on a certification card. Method scope is bounded by the certificates the individual actually holds.

facets.q: Does hiring an outside Level III make our certifications third-party certifications?
facets.a: No. Third-party certification means a body independent of the employer both examines and issues the credential, as ASNT does with its own NDT Level III certificate. An outside Level III working under your written practice produces employer-based certifications that belong to your company, carry your company's name, and stop being valid to your customers if the holder leaves your payroll.

facets.q: Can the outside Level III sign our certification records if our written practice says so?
facets.a: No, and writing it into the practice creates the finding rather than curing it. The written practice is subordinate to the scheme it invokes, and both SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 place certification with the employer. An auditor who sees an agency signature on a certification card will read the written practice next and cite both documents rather than one.

facets.q: Who signs the certification if nobody left in the company is a Level III?
facets.a: A designated officer of the employer signs, and the signature does not require Level III credentials. Certification attests that documented requirements were met, not that the signer evaluated them personally. Name the certifying officer by title in the written practice, state that the approving Level III's qualification records are attached, and keep the outside Level III's examination and grading records in the same file.

facets.q: Does the outside Level III need to be ASNT NDT Level III certified?
facets.a: Under CP-189, yes: employer certification at Level III requires a current ASNT NDT Level III certificate in the applicable method. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer's written practice sets the route, and many practices adopt the ASNT certificate as the qualifying route anyway. Under NAS 410 the Responsible Level 3 must be certified as a Level 3 in one or more methods the employer uses.

facets.q: Can the same outside agency train, examine and audit us?
facets.a: Yes, and paragraph 8.1.1 is an argument for it. That clause bars a candidate from administering their own examination or having a subordinate administer it. In a shop where one internal Level III trained every technician, the independence is thin. A contracted Level III has no reporting line to the candidate, which removes the conflict rather than creating one.

facets.q: What happens to our certifications if we change outside agencies?
facets.a: Nothing, provided the records are yours. Certifications were issued by your company, so an agency change does not touch them. The exposure is documentary: if examination masters, graded papers, procedure approval sheets and qualification files live on the agency's system, you lose the evidence that supports every card you signed. Contract for record ownership and copies held inside your quality system from day one.

sections.heading: Qualify Versus Certify: The Two Words That Decide the Answer
paragraphs: The question "can an outside agency certify my NDT employees" resolves cleanly once you separate two acts that shops use interchangeably. Qualification is evidentiary. It is the training hours delivered, the documented experience in the method, the general examination, the method-specific examination, the practical demonstration on representative hardware, and the current near-vision and colour contrast test. Certification is administrative. It is a signed record in which an employer declares that a named person has met the requirements of that employer's written practice for a stated method and level, on a stated date.

An outside agency can generate every element of the first act. It cannot perform the second, because the second is a statement about a relationship the agency is not part of. This is why auditors phrase the question as "who is your certifying authority" rather than "who trained these people." They expect a person inside your company holding delegated signature authority, supported by a file of qualification evidence that an outside Level III may well have produced from start to finish.

The practical consequence is that outsourcing Level III work does not outsource responsibility. SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7.4 makes the employer responsible for assuring that outside training met the written practice, and the same logic runs through the rest of the document. You buy expertise, examination integrity and audit readiness. You do not buy an escape from ownership of the program, and no contract clause can transfer it.

sections.heading: What an Outside Level III Signs, and What They Never Sign
paragraphs: A well-run outsourced arrangement produces a specific, auditable stack of signed documents. The outside Level III signs the approval block on the written practice, satisfying paragraph 5.5. They sign procedure and technique approvals within the methods they hold. They sign examination cover sheets, question-bank approvals and grading records, satisfying the Section 8 requirement that in-house certification examination questions be approved by the NDT Level III. They sign technical performance evaluation records and the annual program audit report.

There is exactly one document they never sign: the certification record itself, whether that is a wallet card, a certificate of certification or a line in a personnel qualification register. They also never sign anywhere the form asserts "employer." If your template has a single signature line serving both the technical approval and the employer's declaration, split it into two lines before the contract starts rather than after the audit.

A reliable test separates the two categories. If the document asserts a technical fact, such as a candidate scoring 87 percent on a graded specific examination or a procedure meeting the requirements of the referencing code article, the outside Level III is the correct signatory. If the document asserts a status the person holds inside your company, only your company can assert it. Technical facts travel with the expert. Status travels with the employer.

sections.heading: SNT-TC-1A: A Recommended Practice Your Code Turns Into a Requirement
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A is written as guidance for employers building an in-house program, and its 2024 edition continues that framing. Paragraph 1.4 nevertheless states that employers shall not eliminate the basic provisions covering training, experience, examination and recertification. Paragraph 5.1 requires the employer to establish a written practice for the control and administration of NDT personnel training, examination and certification. Paragraph 5.5 requires that written practice to be reviewed and approved by the employer's NDT Level III, and 5.6 requires it to be maintained on file.

The reason it behaves like a mandatory document is invocation. ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120(e) requires NDE personnel to be qualified and certified in accordance with a written practice, with SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 used as the guideline for establishing it. Construction and fabrication codes reach the same place by their own routes. ASME administratively approves specific editions and addendum states, so confirm which edition your code year invokes before your written practice cites one by year.

Everything an outside Level III does fits inside that structure without amending it. The document says "the employer's NDT Level III" and describes duties. It does not say the individual must be a W-2 employee, and it does not create a named post. What it does do, repeatedly, is put the employer's name on the outcome. Read every paragraph asking who is responsible if this is wrong, and the answer never moves.

sections.heading: ANSI/ASNT CP-189: Same Boundary, Tighter Gate
paragraphs: CP-189 is a standard rather than a recommended practice, so its provisions read as requirements once a contract or code invokes it. The boundary on certifying authority is identical to SNT-TC-1A: the employer certifies, and an outside agency does not. Where CP-189 changes the outsourcing calculation is the gate on the Level III themselves. Employer certification at Level III under CP-189 requires the individual to hold a current ASNT NDT Level III certificate in the method concerned.

That single requirement removes the internally examined Level III as an option. You cannot write a practice that qualifies your senior UT technician to Level III on your own examinations and satisfy CP-189 at the same time. You either employ or contract someone who already holds the ASNT credential in each method your program certifies, which is precisely the condition that makes contracting attractive to a shop running four, five or six methods with no realistic path to hiring one person who holds them all.

Method scope becomes the discipline in a CP-189 program. A contracted Level III certified in UT and PT can approve UT and PT procedures and grade UT and PT examinations, and nothing else. Shops running magnetic particle, radiography and eddy current alongside those methods often engage two contractors with complementary certificates, or one agency that fields more than one certified individual. Map methods to certificates in the contract, not in an email.

sections.heading: NAS 410 and the Responsible Level 3: The One Genuine Difference
paragraphs: Aerospace works differently, and this is where most of the confusion originates. NAS 410, published by the Aerospace Industries Association and now at Revision 6, requires the employer to identify in writing a Responsible Level 3 to act on its behalf in matters regarding the NDT qualification and certification process. SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 describe duties attaching to "the employer's NDT Level III" without creating a titled post. NAS 410 creates the post, names its holder in the employer's documentation, and makes that designation itself an auditable artefact.

The qualifying conditions are specific. The Responsible Level 3 must be certified in accordance with the standard as a Level 3 in one or more NDT methods, and must hold a thorough knowledge of the written instructions, codes, specifications and standards the employer uses, together with knowledge of the materials, components, product technologies, methods and techniques the employer actually applies. That second condition is why a purely remote, never-visited arrangement fails on the substance even when it passes on paper. Product knowledge is site knowledge.

Revision 6 also introduced an alternative points-based pathway toward Level 3 qualification, allowing Level 2 personnel to accumulate credit through designated NDT activities. That widens the internal succession route over time, but it does not touch the certifying boundary. Even in aerospace, where the Responsible Level 3 may sit outside the company, the employer certifies its own personnel and the employer answers for the program. Prime contractor flowdowns and accreditation checklists frequently add their own constraints on top, so verify your customer's clauses before signing.

sections.heading: Paragraph 8.1.1 and Why Outsourcing Often Improves Compliance
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A paragraph 8.1.1 states that a certification examination shall not be administered by the candidate themselves or by a subordinate of the candidate. In a large company this is trivially satisfied. In a twelve-person inspection shop with one Level III who wrote the training material, delivered the classroom hours, supervised the on-the-job time and then set the examination, the independence is thin even when nobody has done anything improper. When that Level III is the candidate seeking recertification, the clause bites directly.

A contracted Level III breaks the loop cleanly. There is no reporting relationship in either direction, no shared bonus pool and no supervisory history between examiner and candidate. The same argument applies to the annual or periodic program audit, where an internal Level III is being asked to audit a system they designed and operate. Independence purchased deliberately reads far better in an audit narrative than independence claimed after the fact.

This reframes the outsourcing decision. Shops usually start looking for an outside Level III because they lost one or never had one. The stronger reason to keep the arrangement after the immediate gap closes is that examination integrity and audit independence are structurally easier to demonstrate when the examiner is not on the same organisation chart as the candidate.

sections.heading: Where This Goes Wrong on Audit Day
paragraphs: Five failure modes account for most findings. First, certification cards carrying the agency's name or the contracted Level III's signature in the certifying block. Second, a written practice that names the agency as the certifying authority, which converts a document error into a systemic one because the practice is the governing document. Third, method scope drift, where a contractor certified in ultrasonics and penetrant approves a radiography procedure because they were the Level III on site that week.

Fourth, no evidence on file of the outside Level III's own current certification, recertification date and, where CP-189 applies, their ASNT certificate number and expiry. The auditor will ask for it in the first ten minutes, and an agency letterhead assurance is not the same as a copy of the credential. Fifth, examination records that record only a pass, with no examination version, date, proctor identity, question set reference or graded paper retained. The grading happened off site, so the evidence has to be transferred deliberately.

All five are documentary rather than technical, and all five are cheap to prevent and expensive to remediate. Remediation usually means re-examining personnel whose records cannot be reconstructed, on a schedule set by a customer rather than by you, while the affected work sits in hold status. The cost of that is the real argument for structuring the contract properly at the start.

sections.heading: Structuring the Contract So the Boundary Stays Visible
paragraphs: Name the certifying officer in the written practice by title rather than by person, so a departure does not invalidate the document. Add a short paragraph stating explicitly that Level III technical duties are performed under contract by a named external individual, that their qualification records are held in the quality system, and that certification is executed by the named officer. An auditor who reads that paragraph in the first five minutes rarely spends the next hour probing for the gap.

Define method scope in the contract as a table of methods against the contractor's certificates, with a clause that scope changes require a certificate copy before any approval is signed. Define the deliverable list: written practice approvals, procedure approvals, examination sets, graded papers, technical performance evaluation records, audit reports. Define response times for procedure approval, because a two-week turnaround on a procedure revision stops production just as effectively as having no Level III at all.

Settle record ownership before the first document is produced. Examination masters, question banks, graded papers and qualification files belong inside your quality system, with the agency holding copies rather than originals. Add an exit clause covering handover of all records within a fixed period, and a continuity clause covering what happens if the agency changes the individual assigned to you, since that individual's certificates are what bound your program's scope.

sections.heading: How Atlantis Provides Outsourced Level III Support
paragraphs: Atlantis provides outsourced ASNT Level III services structured around exactly this boundary. We author and approve your written practice, build and maintain method examination banks, proctor and grade examinations, approve NDT procedures and techniques within our certified methods, run technical performance evaluations, and conduct the periodic program audit that keeps you ready for customer and accreditation visits. The engagement is affordable, accessible and fully customizable to the methods and codes your contracts actually invoke.

We do not sign your certification records, and we say so at kickoff rather than at handover. Part of onboarding is restructuring your certification template so the technical approval block and the employer declaration block are separate lines, and identifying the officer in your company who will hold signature authority. Shops that skip that step end up with a technically excellent program that fails on a single line of a form.

If your Level III post is vacant, contested at audit, or spread across more methods than one credential covers, request a demo or a quote at /contact or write to info@atlantisndt.com. Tell us the methods, the codes your customers invoke and the accreditation you hold, and we will map which duties transfer to us and which stay with your certifying officer before any contract is drafted.

faq.q: Is an outside Level III allowed under ASME Section V?
faq.a: Yes. ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120(e) requires personnel to be qualified and certified in accordance with a written practice built using SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 as the guideline. Neither the code nor the referenced schemes require the Level III to be a direct employee. They require the employer to own the written practice and to execute certification.

faq.q: Can one outside Level III cover all our methods?
faq.a: Only within the methods on their own certificate. A Level III certified in ultrasonics cannot approve a radiographic procedure or grade a magnetic particle examination. Multi-method shops either engage an agency that fields several certified individuals or contract two specialists. Record the method-to-certificate mapping in the contract and refresh it whenever either party adds a method.

faq.q: Does an outside Level III have to visit our site?
faq.a: Site presence is what makes several duties defensible. Practical examinations, technical performance evaluations and program audits are difficult to evidence remotely, and NAS 410 explicitly requires the Responsible Level 3 to know the employer's materials, components and product technologies. Written practice drafting, procedure review and question-bank development work well remotely. Split the scope accordingly and schedule the on-site elements in the contract.

faq.q: Does an outside Level III cover API 510, 570 or 653 inspector certification?
faq.a: No, and the distinction matters. API 510, 570 and 653 are individual certifications issued by API through its Individual Certification Programs, earned by the person and held by the person. They are not employer-based certifications and no written practice governs them. An outside Level III has no authority over them, and Atlantis does not provide training toward them.

faq.q: What records prove the outside Level III actually did the work?
faq.a: Keep the signed written practice approval page, copies of the contractor's own certificates with expiry dates, procedure approval sheets bearing their signature and method, examination sets with version and date, graded answer papers, practical examination score sheets naming the examiner, technical performance evaluation records, and the periodic audit report. Store all of it in your quality system rather than relying on the agency's files.

faq.q: If we later hire an internal Level III, do we redo anything?
faq.a: Certifications already issued stand, because your company issued them. Update the written practice to reflect the new approving Level III, record the handover date, and keep the outgoing contractor's approvals and examination records on file as the evidence supporting every certification signed during their tenure. Procedures approved under the previous Level III remain approved until they are revised.

title: Your NDT Level III Resigned: What Stops and What Continues
description: Your NDT Level III resigned. Existing certifications stay valid; the approving authority does not. A 30/60/90-day plan for what stops and what continues.
h1: Your NDT Level III Just Resigned: The First 90 Days
answer: Existing certifications remain valid. The approving authority does not. From the effective date, nobody can certify a new technician, approve or revise a procedure, approve or grade an examination, or sign a written practice revision. Name an interim approving Level III in writing within days, take custody of examination banks and qualification records immediately, and secure permanent authority before the first recertification falls due.
expansion: Certification under SNT-TC-1A is issued by the employer, not by the individual Level III, so every technician certificate your company signed remains valid on its own terms after the Level III walks out. What leaves is authority. Paragraph 5.5 requires the written practice to be reviewed and approved by the employer's NDT Level III. Section 8 requires in-house certification examination questions to be approved by the NDT Level III. With the post vacant, both sentences point at nobody. In practice that means no new hire can be certified, no procedure revision can be approved, no examination can be graded, and no recertification falling due inside the gap can be completed. Section 13 separately deems the departing individual's own employer-based certification revoked on termination of employment. Their personal ASNT certificate travels with them; your records of what they approved do not, and should not. The fix is a written interim designation, not a hiring cycle.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition), paras 5.1, 5.5, 5.6, 8.1.1 and Sections 8, 10, 11, 12, 13; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 (2024); AIA NAS 410 Rev. 6, para 4.5; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1, T-120(e).
