It does not permit the employer's responsibility to be contracted, and it does not permit one employer to certify another employer's people. Rev. 6 was released in December 2025; confirm which revision your prime flows down before rewriting the designation, because the flowed-down revision governs.

facets.q: Can our Responsible Level 3 be an employee of another company?
facets.a: Yes. NAS 410 para 4.5 requires the Responsible Level 3 to be identified in writing and permits that person to be contracted. Shops with no Level 3 on payroll run compliant aerospace programmes on this route every day, and Nadcap AC7114 recognises an external Level 3 approving procedures. The employer remains responsible for assuring the requirements of the standard are met, holds the designation document, holds copies of the Level 3's qualification records, and signs its own employees' certification records.

facets.q: Must the Responsible Level 3 be certified in every method we perform?
facets.a: Yes, for every method they approve. A Level 3 certified in penetrant and magnetic particle cannot approve ultrasonic procedures, cannot approve ultrasonic examination questions, and cannot stand behind an ultrasonic certification. Shops covering four or five methods commonly split the role: one Level 3 named for the methods they hold, a second named for the remainder. The designation document lists the methods against each name, which is exactly what the assessor reads when the personnel list shows a method neither name covers.

facets.q: How often must the Responsible Level 3 be on site?
facets.a: NAS 410 sets no attendance frequency. The obligations set the frequency instead. Practical examinations require the examiner present with the candidate and the specimens. Internal NDT audits and technique reviews require observation of work as performed. Nadcap job audits require the Level 3 available during the assessment. Working backwards from those, most contracted arrangements land on scheduled site visits for examination cycles and audits, with procedure and technique approvals handled remotely against a contracted response time.

facets.q: Does EN 4179 treat the Responsible Level 3 the same way?
facets.a: EN 4179 is the technically equivalent European document and carries the same Responsible Level 3 concept, with one structural difference: Europe operates National Aerospace NDT Boards, and the NANDTB participates in Level 3 qualification and oversight. The United States has no NANDTB, so US aerospace runs employer-based under NAS 410 with primes and Nadcap performing that oversight. A supplier serving both markets writes one written practice that satisfies the stricter route rather than maintaining two programmes.

facets.q: Can we name a Level 3 qualified through ASNT rather than a NANDTB?
facets.a: Yes, in the United States. NAS 410 does not make an ASNT Level III certificate a prerequisite for the role, and a current ASNT Level III certificate in the method satisfies the general examination requirement, which is why the ASNT route dominates US aerospace. What the audit examines is consistency: the qualification route your written practice describes must be the route the Level 3's own file documents, with the examination evidence present rather than assumed from the certificate.

facets.q: What happens to our certifications if the Responsible Level 3 changes?
facets.a: Existing certifications stay valid. The approving authority does not transfer automatically. Issue a new written designation before the outgoing Level 3's last day, transfer custody of the examination bank, answer keys, qualification files and approved procedure set, and have the incoming Level 3 review and re-approve the written practice. The detailed sequence, including what stops the moment the departure takes effect, is at /consulting/ndt-level-3-resigned-what-to-do.

sections.heading: Paragraph 4.5 Is the Whole Difference From SNT-TC-1A
paragraphs: ASNT SNT-TC-1A tells an employer to establish a written practice and to have an NDT Level III approve it, approve the procedures and approve the examinations. It never names that person in the standard's own vocabulary, and it never demands that the employer publish who they are. NAS 410 does both. Paragraph 4.5 requires the employer to identify a Responsible Level 3 in writing. That is a named individual, not a job title, not a department, and not a rotating duty shared between two senior technicians who each cover part of the scope.

The reason aerospace insists on a name is traceability of authority. When a prime contractor asks who approved the technique sheet that inspected their turbine disc, or when a Nadcap assessor asks who decides that a candidate is qualified, the answer resolves to a person with a certification file, a vision record and an examination history. A role title cannot hold a certification. A named individual can, and the entire aerospace qualification chain is built on being able to walk backwards from a part to a person.

The second half of para 4.5 is what makes it commercially workable. The Responsible Level 3 may be contracted. A shop of twelve people performing penetrant and magnetic particle on aerospace parts does not need a full-time Level 3 salary to hold a compliant designation, and NAS 410 was written knowing that. The employer remains responsible for assuring the requirements of the standard are met, which is a different obligation from performing every technical act personally.

sections.heading: Who Qualifies to Hold the Designation
paragraphs: The holder is qualified as a Level 3 in each method they will cover, with the qualification supported by records rather than reputation. In the United States that route runs through ASNT: a current ASNT Level III certificate in the method satisfies the general examination requirement, and the employer's written practice defines what else is required. In Europe the NANDTB participates directly. Either way, the file must show the examinations behind the certificate, not only the certificate itself, because the assessor tests the route your written practice claims against the evidence in the folder.

Method coverage is the constraint shops trip over. A Level 3 certified in PT and MT is unable to approve UT procedures, unable to approve UT examination questions, and unable to stand behind a UT certification, regardless of how experienced they are with the method in practice. Where a shop performs four or five methods, the designation splits: one name covering the methods they hold, another name covering the rest. The designation document lists methods against each name so the coverage is visible on one page.

The holder also needs the standing to act. NAS 410 expects the Responsible Level 3 to be in charge of the NDT programme and to interface with other companies, auditors and regulatory bodies on the company's behalf. A contracted holder therefore needs a contract that grants that standing explicitly, and an internal reporting line that does not allow a production manager to override a technical decision. Where the designation exists on paper but the authority does not, the arrangement fails on the first disagreement about a rejected part.

sections.heading: What the Written Designation Must State
paragraphs: Four elements make a designation auditable. The individual's full name and their Level 3 certification credentials. The methods covered, listed explicitly rather than implied by the scope of the business. The authority granted, written as verbs the assessor can test: approves the written practice, approves procedures and technique sheets, prepares and approves examination material, designates examination administrators and vision examiners, performs or oversees internal NDT audits. And an effective date, with the signature of a company officer who has the standing to grant that authority.

The designation belongs in two places. It is stated in the written practice, which is the controlled document the assessor reads first, and it exists as a separately signed management memo or contract schedule that can be produced on its own. Keeping both aligned is the maintenance task shops fail. When the written practice is revised for an unrelated reason and the Level 3 name is carried forward from the previous revision without checking, the document quietly asserts something that stopped being true.

What the designation must not do is assign the certification signature to the contracted holder. NAS 410 makes the employer responsible for certifying its own employees, and an employer cannot certify for another employer. A designation that grants the outside Level 3 authority to sign certification records creates a nonconformance in the document itself, before a single technician has been certified under it. The full authority boundary is set out at /consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do.

sections.heading: What the Responsible Level 3 Is Accountable For
paragraphs: The written practice comes first, because everything else is audited against it. The Responsible Level 3 approves it, and that approval means the document describes a programme they will defend: the training hours, the experience hours, the examination structure, the recertification interval, the vision cadence, and the designated administrators. Where the written practice promises more than NAS 410 requires, the Responsible Level 3 has committed the company to the higher figure, and that is the figure the assessor uses.

Procedures and technique sheets come next, one approval per document, per method, per revision. This is the highest-volume obligation and the one that generates the most findings, because engineering issues revisions and the re-approval lags. A contracted arrangement handles this by defining a response time for approvals in the agreement, so a revision cannot go into production while waiting. Annual technique review, where the written practice promises it, is a scheduled event with a record, not a background intention.

Examinations are the third pillar: preparing or approving the general, specific and practical material, approving every question, designating who administers and grades, and standing behind the result. The full structure of that oversight, including the rule that no candidate may have their examination administered by themselves or a subordinate, is set out at /consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight. The fourth pillar is surveillance: internal NDT audits, technician performance monitoring, and the annual proficiency checks your written practice commits to.

sections.heading: The Outside-Agency Route, Written as a Contract
paragraphs: A contracted designation succeeds or fails on the agreement behind it. Name the methods covered. List the delegated activities individually rather than as "Level III services": written practice approval, procedure and technique sheet approval, examination preparation, administration and grading, vision examiner designation and training, internal NDT audits, annual technique review. State a response time for approvals in business days. And name the availability commitment for scheduled events, including your Nadcap audit dates, which are published well in advance and therefore contractible.

Records custody is the clause shops forget and assessors ask about first. The examination bank, answer keys, marked papers, qualification files and approved procedure set are the employer's property, held at the employer's premises or in a system the employer controls, with the agency holding working copies. Write it that way. The alternative is the failure mode that turns a routine contract change into a rebuild: the agency departs, and the examination material and half the qualification evidence depart with them.

Copies of the Level 3's own qualification evidence live in your personnel files, not at the consultancy. Certification in each covered method, the examination evidence behind it, a current vision record, and the signed designation naming them for your facility. Assessors ask for this file early in an AC7114 audit and "our consultant keeps those" is written up, because the employer carries the responsibility for assuring the standard is met. The audit-readiness detail sits at /consulting/nadcap-ac7114-audit-readiness.

sections.heading: The One Authority the Contract Cannot Move
paragraphs: Certification is an act of the employer. NAS 410 holds the employer responsible for the certification of its own employees and forbids one employer certifying for another. A contracted Responsible Level 3 qualifies your people: they approve the training, verify the experience, approve and grade the examinations, and confirm the vision status. An officer of your company then signs the certification record stating that this employee is certified to this level in this method under your written practice. Two signatures, two different parties, and the distinction survives every audit.

Shops collapse this because the qualification work is the substantive part and the signature feels administrative. It is the reverse. The signature is what makes the certification yours, which is what makes it valid when the outside agency's contract ends. Certification records signed by a consultancy have to be reissued, and reissuing them means revisiting every file to confirm the underlying qualification evidence still supports the claim. Getting the signature right at the outset costs nothing; getting it wrong costs a full records remediation.

sections.heading: One Name, Several Methods and Several Sites
paragraphs: Multi-method shops split the designation by method and multi-site companies face a harder question. NAS 410 does not require a Responsible Level 3 per site, but it does require the named person to be in charge of the programme they are named for. A single name across four sites works where one written practice governs all four, records are held in one controlled system, and the person actually reaches each site for examinations and audits. It fails where sites run local variants of the procedures and the name on the document has not visited in two years.

The practical test is whether the named person can answer for any file pulled at any site without a phone call. Where they cannot, split the designation and write the split into the written practice explicitly, with each name carrying its own site and method list. Assessors accept a distributed structure that is documented. They write up a centralised structure that is fictional, because the finding is not about the geography, it is about the authority being nominal.

sections.heading: Replacing a Responsible Level 3 Without a Gap
paragraphs: Certifications already issued stay valid when the Responsible Level 3 changes. The approving authority is what lapses, and it lapses on the effective date rather than when the paperwork catches up. From that moment nobody can certify a new technician, approve a procedure revision, approve or grade an examination, or approve a written practice change until a new designation exists in writing. Shops discover this when a technique sheet needs a revision on day three of the gap and there is nobody empowered to sign it.

Overlap the two holders wherever the timing permits. Issue the incoming designation before the outgoing last day, transfer custody of the examination bank, answer keys, qualification files and the approved procedure set as a documented handover, and have the incoming Level 3 review and re-approve the written practice under their own name rather than inheriting an approval. Where an overlap is impossible, a contracted interim designation closes the gap in days. The full recovery sequence is at /consulting/ndt-level-3-resigned-what-to-do.

sections.heading: How Atlantis Holds the Designation
paragraphs: Atlantis holds Responsible Level 3 designations under contract for aerospace suppliers that have no Level 3 on payroll and for shops whose employed Level 3 does not cover every method they perform. The engagement starts by reading your written practice against NAS 410 and against what your primes flowed down, then rewriting the designation, the authority statement and the records custody terms so the arrangement is auditable on its face rather than defensible only in conversation.

From there we approve procedures and technique sheets in the covered methods against a contracted response time, prepare and approve examination material as a controlled bank, administer and grade examinations on scheduled site visits, designate and train your vision examiner, run the internal NDT audit, and attend Nadcap assessments booked against dates in the agreement. Your company signs the certification records. The retainer structure is described at /consulting/ndt-consulting-level-iii. Ask for a quote and we will scope it against your methods, headcount and audit calendar.

faq.q: Does SNT-TC-1A require a Responsible Level 3 as well?
faq.a: No. SNT-TC-1A requires a written practice approved by an NDT Level III and makes that Level III responsible for approving examination questions, procedures and the programme, but it creates no named role with the title Responsible Level 3 and no obligation to publish who holds it. NAS 410 para 4.5 adds both. A shop moving from general industry into aerospace usually already has the substance and simply lacks the written designation, which is a one-document fix.

faq.q: Can one person be Responsible Level 3 for two different companies?
faq.a: Yes. Contracted Level 3s routinely hold the designation for several suppliers at once, and NAS 410 permits it because the designation is an employer-side document rather than an exclusivity arrangement. What NAS 410 forbids is one employer certifying another employer's employees, which is a separate rule. The practical limit is availability: each designation carries examination cycles, audit attendance and approval turnaround, and a Level 3 holding more designations than their calendar supports produces late approvals, which produce findings.

faq.q: Does the Responsible Level 3 approve our internal NDT audits?
faq.a: Yes, where your written practice assigns internal NDT audits to the role, which most aerospace written practices do. AC7114 assesses internal NDT audits as a subject area, so the audit plan, the completed audit records, the findings raised and their closure all become audit evidence in their own right. A contracted holder performing your internal audit brings an advantage: they are auditing a programme they approved but did not operate, so the observations are genuinely independent of daily production pressure.

faq.q: Do we need a NANDTB if we operate only in the United States?
faq.a: No. The United States has no National Aerospace NDT Board. US aerospace suppliers run employer-based certification under NAS 410, with prime contractors and Nadcap performing the oversight role that a NANDTB performs in Europe under EN 4179. If you supply European primes or hold EN 4179 obligations flowed down through a contract, the NANDTB route enters through that contract rather than through your US operations, and the written practice must then satisfy both.

faq.q: What does Atlantis need in order to hold the designation for us?
faq.a: Your current written practice, your procedure and technique sheet set, your personnel list with methods and levels, the qualification files as they stand, and the specification flow-down from your primes. From those we produce a gap report, a redrafted designation and authority statement, and a schedule of what needs rebuilding before your next audit. Ask for a scoping call and a quote, and the scope is set by your methods, your headcount and your audit date rather than by a standard package.

title: Nobody May Administer Their Own NDT Certification Exam
description: SNT-TC-1A 8.1.1 bars self-administered and subordinate-administered exams. Who writes, approves, administers and grades each part, and what records survive.
h1: Writing, Approving, Administering and Grading NDT Qualification Examinations
answer: SNT-TC-1A 8.1.1 states that in no case shall an examination be administered by oneself or by a subordinate. That single sentence decides the architecture. The Level III responsible for the method approves every question, the general, specific and practical parts are separately prepared and graded, each part requires 70 percent and the composite 80 percent, and the papers themselves are retained, not just the scores.
expansion: Certification examinations fail audits in a predictable order. The score sheet exists and the papers do not. The composite is recorded and the three part scores are not. The practical was administered by the shift supervisor who also trained the candidate and signs the candidate's timesheet. The specific examination cites a procedure at a revision superseded two years earlier. None of these are competence problems, and all four are written up. The structure that survives scrutiny separates four roles shops routinely collapse into one person: who writes the questions, who approves them, who sits with the candidate, and who grades the result. A contracted Level III separates them by construction, because that person supervises nobody in the building and reports to nobody the candidate outranks. That separation is an audit argument before it is ever a commercial one.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024), Section 8 Examinations, para 8.1.1 (no examination administered by oneself or by a subordinate), approval of examination questions by the NDT Level III, the 80 percent composite with no individual examination below 70 percent, and paras 5.1, 5.5 and 5.6 on the written practice; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 (2024); AIA NAS 410 Rev. 6 (December 2025) and Rev. 5 (September 2020), including the sequencing of the specific examination after 75 percent and the practical after 100 percent of required experience hours, and the vision examination requirements.

table.note: NAS 410 Rev. 5 added sequencing: the specific examination is administered after at least 75 percent of required experience hours and the practical after 100 percent. That only proves out if the experience log carries dated entries to compare the examination dates against.

facets.q: Can our Level III administer the examination for someone they trained?
facets.a: Yes, provided the candidate is not the Level III themselves and is not the Level III's own subordinate in the sense SNT-TC-1A 8.1.1 addresses. Training and examining are separate acts, and the standard bars self-administration and subordinate administration rather than instructor involvement. The practice that draws scrutiny is a supervisor who trains the candidate, administers the examination, grades it and signs their performance review, because every check on the result runs through one person with an interest in it.

facets.q: Who may administer a Level III candidate's own examination?
facets.a: An outside agency, ASNT, or a NANDTB where one exists. Never the candidate, and never someone who reports to the candidate. This is where the rule bites hardest, because a shop's only Level III cannot examine themselves into a higher method and cannot have their own Level II run the paper. The route is a third party, and it is the same reason many shops contract Level III oversight in the first place: the independence is structural rather than asserted.

facets.q: How many questions does each examination part require?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A publishes minimum question counts by method and level in its examination table, and your written practice states the counts you use. Those counts must meet or exceed the table, and the assessor compares the paper in the file against the number your own document promised. Where the written practice says forty general questions and the retained paper has twenty-eight, the finding is against your written practice rather than against the standard, which is the harder one to argue away.

facets.q: Does recertification require a new practical examination?
facets.a: Your written practice decides, within the bounds SNT-TC-1A sets, and it must decide explicitly. Recertification runs at intervals your written practice defines, with SNT-TC-1A recommending a maximum of five years, and the evidence route is either re-examination or documented evidence of continued satisfactory performance. Whichever route you choose, the record must exist for each cycle. The most common finding is a recertification date advanced on a tracker with no examination, no performance evidence and no Level III signature behind it.

facets.q: Can an outside agency write our examination bank and also grade it?
facets.a: Yes. SNT-TC-1A accepts an outside agency preparing, administering and grading qualification examinations, and CP-189 takes the same position. The boundary is the certification decision: the agency qualifies, an officer of the employer certifies, and the certification record carries the employer's signature. Using one agency across writing, administering and grading is the arrangement most likely to satisfy 8.1.1, because nobody involved sits in the candidate's reporting line. The full authority split is at /consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do.

facets.q: What identifies a practical examination specimen adequately?
facets.a: A control number unique to that specimen, a record of the discontinuities present with their type and location, the material and configuration, and a controlled storage location. The examination record then states which specimens the candidate examined and what they detected and reported against what was actually present. A practical recorded as "passed practical, 85 percent" with no specimen identification cannot be reconstructed by anyone, which is precisely why assessors read the practical file before the written ones.

sections.heading: One Sentence Sets the Whole Architecture
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A 8.1.1 states that in no case shall an examination be administered by oneself or by a subordinate. It is the shortest requirement in the examination section and the one with the widest consequences, because it forces a separation of duties that small NDT departments have no natural way to produce. A shop with one Level III, two Level IIs and four technicians has a single technical authority who trains everyone, supervises everyone, and would otherwise write, administer and grade every examination in the building.

The rule exists because a qualification examination is a control, and a control administered by the person whose work it validates has stopped being a control. The examination result feeds a certification record that a customer relies on when they accept an inspection report on a pressure vessel or a turbine disc. Removing the conflict of interest is not an administrative nicety; it is the reason the certification carries weight outside the company that issued it.

NAS 410 carries the same prohibition into aerospace and applies it to the Level 3 candidate specifically: the examination shall not be administered by the candidate or by a subordinate. So the aerospace shop and the general industry shop reach the same conclusion by different routes. Somebody outside the reporting line has to run the examination, and once that is accepted, the rest of the design follows from it.

sections.heading: Four Documents, Four Distinct Roles
paragraphs: A qualification examination is not one event. It is a general examination on the method, a specific examination on your procedures and equipment, a practical examination with real specimens, and a current vision examination, plus a composite calculation that combines the first three. Each has a different author, a different administrator and a different retention profile, and shops that treat the set as a single pass or fail lose the ability to demonstrate any part of it under scrutiny.

The four roles worth separating are: who writes the questions, who approves them, who sits with the candidate, and who grades the result. SNT-TC-1A requires the NDT Level III responsible for the method to approve every question, which fixes the second role. The 8.1.1 restriction fixes the third. Writing and grading can sit with the same person as approval, but the further they are distributed across independent parties, the less an assessor has to probe.

Vision is the role most often forgotten, because it feels medical rather than technical. It is neither: it is a designated act. The Responsible Level 3 designates who administers vision examinations and trains them, or the examination goes to an eye care professional. A vision result recorded without a named examiner is an orphan record, and it appears in personnel files far more often than any other kind of gap because nobody owns it.

sections.heading: The General Examination
paragraphs: The general examination tests method knowledge independent of your shop: physics of the method, equipment principles, variables affecting sensitivity, and the interpretation fundamentals for the level being examined. Its question set is stable across years, which makes it the easiest part to build once and maintain, and the easiest part to buy from an outside agency working to your written practice. What is not optional is Level III approval of every question, method by method, and that approval has a date attached.

The retention obligation is where general examinations quietly fail. Shops keep a score and discard the paper, or keep a paper and lose the answer key, at which point the score is unverifiable. Retain the question set as issued, the key, the candidate's marked responses and the part score. Where the examination is delivered electronically, retain a printable record of the questions presented, the answers given and the key applied, because a system screenshot showing a percentage proves nothing about which questions were asked.

Question banks need a review cycle for the same reason procedures do. Equipment changes, methods evolve, and a general examination written a decade ago tests knowledge nobody uses. Treat the bank as a controlled document with an owner, a revision history and a scheduled review, and record the Level III's re-approval each cycle. That single control also protects you against the failure where all examination material lived on the laptop of a Level III who has since left.

sections.heading: The Specific Examination
paragraphs: The specific examination tests what the candidate needs to know to work in your building: your written procedures, your equipment, your techniques, your acceptance criteria, and the codes and specifications your customers flow down. It is the examination an outside agency cannot supply off the shelf, because the source material is your procedure set. That dependency is exactly what makes it useful evidence, and exactly what makes it go stale.

Every specific question traces to a procedure at a revision. When the procedure is revised, the questions drawn from it must be reviewed and the traceability updated. An assessor reading a specific examination that cites a procedure revision superseded two years ago concludes that the examination bank has never been reviewed against the current document set, and that conclusion reaches beyond the one file in front of them. Record the procedure revision on the question set itself so the check takes seconds.

NAS 410 sequences this examination against experience: it is administered after at least 75 percent of the required experience hours have accumulated. That sequencing is auditable only where the experience log carries dated entries. A retrospective log signed on certification day cannot demonstrate that the specific examination came after 75 percent, because there is nothing to compare the examination date against. Hours logging and examination scheduling are therefore the same problem, handled by the same tracker.

sections.heading: The Practical Examination: Where Files Are Thinnest
paragraphs: The practical examination is the strongest evidence of competence in the file and the weakest record in most shops. It should identify each specimen by control number, state the discontinuities present in that specimen by type and location, record what the candidate detected and how they reported it, capture the instrument and settings used, and carry the checklist the examiner scored line by line. Where the practical required the candidate to write or interpret a technique, that work product belongs in the file too.

Specimen control is what makes the record reconstructable years later. Specimens need unique numbers, characterised flaw sets, controlled storage and a log of who examined which set and when. Shops that rotate a single well-known set through every candidate produce results that are indistinguishable from a memorised answer, and experienced assessors ask how the specimen set is controlled precisely because the answer is diagnostic of how seriously the whole programme is run.

The administration restriction bites hardest here, because a practical requires someone physically present with the candidate for an extended period, and the person most naturally available is the supervisor who trained them. That is the arrangement 8.1.1 exists to prevent where the supervisor is also the candidate's reporting line. Assign a designee outside that line, document their competence and their instruction in administering and grading, and record the designee's name on the practical record itself.

sections.heading: Grading: 80 Composite With No Part Below 70
paragraphs: The grading rule is arithmetic and unforgiving: a composite grade of at least 80 percent, with no individual examination scoring below 70 percent. NAS 410 applies the same structure to the general, specific and practical parts. A candidate scoring 95, 90 and 68 has a composite above 80 and still fails, because one part fell below the floor. A file that records only the composite cannot demonstrate compliance with the second half of the rule, which is why the composite calculation showing all three part scores is the record, not the composite alone.

Grading criteria for the practical need writing down before the examination, not decided afterwards. Define what counts as detection, what counts as correct characterisation, what counts as correct location and sizing within tolerance, and how a missed indication is weighted against a false call. Then score against that written scheme. An examiner scoring a practical from experience produces a defensible result and an indefensible record, and the audit reads the record.

Failures need documenting as thoroughly as passes. Where a candidate fails, the file shows the result, the retraining or additional experience required before re-examination, the waiting period your written practice specifies, and the second examination as a distinct event with its own paper. Shops that quietly re-examine the same day and file only the passing result create a gap between the certification date and the evidence supporting it that surfaces the moment anyone counts the papers.

sections.heading: Designees: Delegation That Survives an Audit
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A allows the Level III to delegate administration and grading to a designee, with a condition attached: the designee has received documented, appropriate instruction from the NDT Level III in the proper administration and grading of qualification examinations before conducting them independently. That documented instruction is a record. It states who was instructed, by whom, on what date, covering what content, and it lives in the designee's file rather than in the Level III's memory of having explained it once.

Choose designees for independence as much as for competence. The useful test is whether the designee has any influence over the candidate's pay, shift, assignments or performance review. Where they do, 8.1.1 is in play regardless of how carefully the examination is run. Where they do not, the examination stands on its own. In small departments this often means the designee sits in quality rather than production, which is a structural answer to a structural problem.

Record the designee on every examination they administer, not just in the delegation letter. The assessor reading a candidate's file asks who administered this examination and what authorised them to do so, and the file should answer both questions without anyone leaving the room. A name on the paper plus an instruction record in that person's own file closes the loop, and it closes it for every candidate they ever examine.

sections.heading: Retention: Keep the Papers, Not the Summary
paragraphs: The retained record set for one certification is larger than most shops expect: the general paper, key and marked responses; the specific paper, key, marked responses and the source procedure revision; the practical checklist, specimen identification, discontinuity sheet, instrument and settings and the candidate's written results; the part scores and composite calculation; the current vision report with its examiner named; the dated experience log; and the certification record signed by an officer of the employer. Each element answers a question the others cannot.

Retention duration follows two rules that operate together. Your written practice states the retention period you commit to, and that commitment is what an auditor holds you to. NAS 410 requires the employer to maintain certification records while the certification is in effect, which means a five-year certification carries a five-year floor on the supporting evidence at minimum, and recertification history extends the useful life further. Where a customer contract specifies longer, the contract governs.

Custody matters as much as duration. Records held only on an individual's machine, or only at an outside agency, are records you cannot produce on audit day. Hold them in a system the employer controls, with the agency holding working copies, and write that into the service agreement. This is the single clause that turns a Level III transition from a rebuild into a handover, and the recovery sequence when it was never written is at /consulting/ndt-level-3-resigned-what-to-do.

sections.heading: Why Independence Argues for an Outside Level III
paragraphs: Read 8.1.1 as an organisational design constraint rather than a compliance line and the case for outside oversight writes itself. The prohibition requires an examiner who is neither the candidate nor anyone reporting to the candidate. In a department of six, the pool of people satisfying that test while also being competent to grade the method is frequently empty. A contracted Level III is outside the reporting structure entirely: they supervise nobody, they report to nobody the candidate outranks, and they carry no interest in the outcome.

The same independence solves the case that has no internal answer at all: qualifying a Level III. The candidate cannot administer their own examination and cannot have a subordinate do it, so a shop promoting its senior Level II into the Level III role must go outside for that examination regardless of what else it handles internally. Once an outside agency is engaged for that, extending the engagement across the examination bank costs less than maintaining two parallel systems.

There is a records benefit that shows up on audit day. An outside Level III delivers examination material as a controlled deliverable, with question sets, keys, graded papers and retention terms defined in the agreement, because that is how the engagement is scoped. The bank does not live on anyone's laptop, and it does not leave when a person does. The scope and boundary of that arrangement is described at /consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do and the retainer structure at /consulting/ndt-consulting-level-iii.

sections.heading: How Atlantis Runs Examination Oversight
paragraphs: Atlantis builds and holds examination programmes for NDT employers under a written practice we review or rewrite first, because the examination structure must match what that document promises. We prepare general and specific question sets by method and level, approve them as the responsible Level III, characterise and control practical specimens, define written grading criteria before anyone sits the examination, and administer and grade on scheduled site visits. Your company signs the certification records, and the material stays in a system you control.

Where you need one examination rather than a programme, we run it as a discrete engagement: a Level II qualifying in a new method, a Level III candidate who cannot be examined internally, or a recertification cycle that fell due while you had no approving authority. Where you need the whole records position rebuilt ahead of an audit, that work is described at /consulting/nadcap-ac7114-audit-readiness. Ask for a demo of the examination and records structure, or a quote scoped to your methods, levels and headcount.

faq.q: Are online proctored NDT certification examinations acceptable?
faq.a: For the general and specific parts, yes, where your written practice describes the delivery method and the records requirement is met in full: the questions presented, the answers given, the key applied, the part score, and the identity of the administrator. The practical examination is not deliverable this way, because it requires the candidate physically handling instruments and characterised specimens under observation. A shop running written parts remotely still schedules practicals on site with an examiner present.

faq.q: Does an ASNT Level III certificate replace our employer examinations?
faq.a: No. An ASNT Level III certificate is third-party evidence of method knowledge and, under NAS 410, a current certificate in the method satisfies the general examination requirement. It does not satisfy the specific examination, because that tests your procedures, your equipment and your customer requirements, and no third party can examine a candidate on documents they have never seen. Employer certification remains an act of the employer regardless of what third-party credentials the candidate holds.

faq.q: Who grades the practical if our only Level III is the candidate?
faq.a: An outside agency or another employer's Level III engaged for the purpose. SNT-TC-1A 8.1.1 and NAS 410 both bar the candidate from administering their own examination and bar a subordinate from doing it, which removes every internal option in a single-Level-III shop. This is the most common entry point into contracted Level III services: a shop needs one examination it cannot lawfully run itself, and discovers the engagement also solves procedure approval and audit attendance.

faq.q: How long must examination records be kept?
faq.a: For at least the period your written practice states, and for as long as the certification supported by them remains in effect. Those two rules operate together: a written practice promising a shorter period than the certification's own life creates a contradiction the auditor resolves against you. Set the retention period to the certification interval plus one full cycle so recertification history stays intact, and confirm no customer contract specifies longer before finalising the figure.

faq.q: Can the same examination paper be used for multiple candidates?
faq.a: Yes, and most banks are built that way. What matters is control: the paper is a controlled document with a revision and a Level III approval, the answer key is held separately from the candidates, and each candidate's marked responses are retained individually. Where a small set of specimens or papers circulates repeatedly, rotate variants and review the bank on a schedule, because an examination everyone in the building has memorised measures recall rather than method knowledge.
